steps: Check local rules first

Confirm clearances, floor protection and approvals with the local building officials before you start. The data plate is on the back of the stove; do not connect to any air distribution duct or system.
Unpack & fit the legs

Lay the flattened carton down as a work surface, take the legs and bolts out of the stove, lay it on its back and unscrew it from the pallet. Bolt the legs on with the supplied bolts (not the pallet bolts) and lift it upright without loading the back legs.
Check loose parts & baffle
Fire bricks firmly in place, air control moving freely, baffle and its insulation seated as pictured. The glove and ceramic flue connection gasket are in the ashpan or firebox area.

After unpacking, check that the fire bricks are firmly in position and have not shifted in transit, and that the air control works freely.

Before the first fire, make sure the baffle and the insulation over it are placed correctly. The manual shows the positions only as pictures (pp. 5–6): lead the vertical baffle through the door, set it in position, and place the baffle insulation on it.

A Morsø glove and the ceramic flue connection gasket are standard accessories, usually found in the ashpan or firebox area.
Chimney

Dedicated flue: masonry with flue liner or listed HT factory-built (UL-103-1985; ULC S-629 in Canada), min. 6 inches and not significantly larger, at least 16 feet recommended. Support it independently of the stove.
Chimney connector

6 inches (150mm), 24 MSG black or blue single-wall or listed double-wall, never galvanized; at least three screws at each joint. Max 3 feet horizontal (recommended) and 8 feet total, no more than two 90 degree turns, rising 1/4 inch per foot toward the chimney.
Position for clearances

Use the clearance table for your connector type and shields (pp. 10–11). Never within 8 inches of combustibles at the sides or 16 inches above the top; 4 inches or more recommended to non-combustible walls.
Floor protection
Non-combustible protector beneath the stove, 16" to the front in the US (450 mm in Canada). For the US side extension, the manual gives both 6" and 8".

The floor protector must be non-combustible and extend beneath the stove.

Front16" US · 450 mm Canada
Sides6" (table) or 8" (diagram, text) US · 200 mm Canada
Back0" min. US · 200 mm Canada
Note: p. 11 gives the US side extension as 6" in the floor-protection table, and as 8" in the diagram and the text on the same page.
Room & air supply
Keep furniture 30 inches away. Add a fresh-air inlet of 2 square inches (1250 square mm) unless the room gets enough air already. Do not install in a mobile home.
First fire
Keep the first fire small so the paint cures and the main plates settle; ventilate the room while the paint gives off fumes.

panels.title: Smoke spills or fire won't respond
items: Smoke or fumes on lighting or reloading, or no response → poor draft, almost certainly; upgrade the flue system
In a very few cases → not enough fresh air getting into the room
Smoke on reloading → open the door 1–2" first and wait a few seconds for flue pressure to equalise
Flue section too large → gases cool; sluggish or unpredictable performance

panels.title: Suddenly sluggish
items: Soot fall around the flue collar or in the flue/chimney
Overly dry, gray wood → back-puffing and sluggishness

panels.title: Dirty or misting glass
items: Fuel too wet (spits or sizzles, glass persistently mists up)
Logs too large or not split
Combustion temperatures too low, or stove run too slowly
Too vigorous burning in contact with cold surfaces when lighting

panels.title: Over-firing & wear
items: Any part glowing, or flue temperature above 450° C (750°F) → over-firing
Baffle distorted by an overfire → efficiency compromised; replace
Fast internal wear → persistent heavy firing, soot and ashes left to accumulate
Door hard to close or air leaking in, fire less controllable → hardened door gasket; replace

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
A cold stove needs lots of air to get going. Morsø recommends the top-down method: it is the most environmentally friendly way to light, and it minimizes soot on the glass.

  1. Use about 2–4 lbs of dry kindling sticks and two firelighters. Place the firelighters directly under the top layer of kindling.
  2. Open the air control on the door fully.
  3. Light the fire.
  4. Close the door most of the way, leaving it open an inch or two so plenty of air gets in. Don't leave the stove while the door is open.
  5. After about 5–10 minutes, when the chimney is warm, close the door. A good layer of embers forms after about 15–20 minutes.

Build the fire directly on the floor of the firebox, not on a grate or andirons. If you can, keep a 1–1.5 inch layer of ash on the floor for insulation.

Your very first fire

Keep it small, so the paint can cure and the main plates can settle into place. The paint gives off some fumes, so ventilate the room.

Never use chemicals or fluids to start the fire.

reload.title: Reloading the stove
reload.html:
Add wood while there is still a bed of glowing embers.

  1. Open the door gently, just 1–2 inches. Wait a few seconds for the pressure in the flue to even out, then open it fully. This stops smoke spilling out, especially when the draft is poor.
  2. Use the poker to spread the embers across the firebox floor, with most of them toward the front.
  3. Add the wood. Morsø recommends a load of 4 lbs (2 pieces) up to 7 lbs (5 pieces).
  4. Close the door and leave the air control fully open. The new wood should catch in a minute or two.
  5. After a few minutes, set the air control for the heat you want.
Keep the wood low. Always keep the load below the lowest secondary air nozzles. The space in front of and above them is only for burning off the gases.
Note: p. 16 gives the maximum recommended load as 3.5 kg/7 lbs (approx 5 split logs); p. 24 says to refuel with 2 - 3 pieces, no more than 2 - 2.5 kg.

Don't open the door while the fire is burning hard. If new logs don't catch, in an extreme case the flue gases can ignite, so make sure there is a good layer of embers first.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
Your stove has two air supplies.

  • Primary air is the one you control, with the spinner on the door. Opening it lets preheated air into the firebox through the airwash system above the glass.
  • Secondary air is fed into the gases above the fire for a cleaner, more efficient burn. It is fixed open and can't be adjusted.

More heat or less

Less heat: fewer logs and less air. More heat: more wood and more air. Either way, keep a good layer of embers.

Open the air fully to light the fire and right after you reload. A few minutes after reloading, set it for the heat you want. Clear, yellow flames tell you the fire is getting enough air.

Burning too slowly puts soot on the glass and lets creosote build up in the chimney.
Leave the low setting alone. The stove has a minimum low burn rate set at the factory. Altering it is against federal regulations.

wood.title: Choosing & seasoning wood
wood.html:
Burn only natural wood that is well seasoned, dry and untreated. The stove is listed for wood only.

Lengthmax 12 inches (30 cm)
Maker's website: Log Size 18".
Thicknessapprox. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm)
Weight per piecearound 2 lbs
Moistureno more than 20%
Note: p. 13 gives the log thickness as approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm) in section; p. 24 says the split wood should be 8 - 12 cm thick.

Seasoning

Split the wood once it's cut to length so the moisture can escape. Stack it under cover somewhere airy. Some softwoods dry in one good summer; oak, maple and elm can take up to 18 months. The Morsø Moisture Meter (part # 62929900) checks it easily.

Dry wood feels light and shows cracks running out from the center at the ends. If it spits or sizzles and the glass keeps misting up, it isn't dry enough. Very dry, gray wood can cause back-puffing and a sluggish fire.

Never burn driftwood from the sea (its salt causes corrosion), construction wood that may be treated with chemicals, or garbage. Don't stack wood inside the stove's clearances.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Run at the right temperatures, the glass should stay fairly clean. Dirt that settles while you light the fire mostly burns off as it heats up.

For deposits that won't burn off

  • Wait until the glass is cold. Never clean it hot.
  • Use Morsø glass cleaner, following its instructions.
  • Never use abrasive cleaners on the glass.

Why it gets dirty

  • The wood is too wet.
  • The logs are too large or not split.
  • The fire is burning too cool.
Cracked or broken glass? Don't use the stove until the glass is replaced. Use only Morsø's high-temperature ceramic glass, from your Morsø dealer. Avoid striking the glass or slamming the door.
Old ceramic glass can't go in ordinary glass recycling. Hand it in at a recycling station as ceramic glass.

ash.title: Removing the ash
ash.html:
A little ash helps: if you can, keep a 1–1.5 inch layer on the firebox floor to insulate the fire. Remove the rest like this:

  1. Open the front door and take the ash out with a shovel.
  2. Put it in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  3. Set the closed container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until you dispose of it.
  4. If you'll bury the ash or spread it outdoors, keep it in the closed container until every cinder has cooled completely.
Never empty the stove while it's burning, and never use a household or shop vacuum to remove the ash.
Soot and ash left to build up wear out the inside of the stove faster.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
Slow fires give off tar and vapors that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. If creosote catches fire, it burns extremely hot.

How often

  • Inspect the chimney and chimney connector at least once every two months during the heating season. Remove any creosote you find.
  • When the stove is new, check for soot above the baffle plate and around the flue outlet about once a month.
  • Clean the chimney all the way to the top after each heating season, and inspect it before the next one for bird's nests or other blockages.

Doing it yourself

Let the stove cool completely, then use a mirror to look up through the flue collar into the chimney. Sweep with a brush the same size and shape as the flue liner. If you can't inspect or clean it yourself, call your Morsø dealer or a professional chimney sweep.

Chimney fire? Act promptly: close the air control, get everyone out of the house, and call the fire department.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
The stove is hot while it's burning, and touching it can burn skin. Keep children, clothing and furniture away.

  • Keep furniture at least 30 inches away, and the same for drying clothes, newspapers and firewood.
  • Burn only with the door fully closed. Never leave the stove unattended with the door open: smoke and flames can be drawn out.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire. Keep them away from the stove.
  • Don't burn garbage. Never burn overnight.

Signs it's too hot

Do not over-fire the stove. If any part of the stove or chimney connector glows, you are over-firing. That can cause a house fire or permanently damage the stove. A Morsø Flue Gas Thermometer (part No. 62901200) on the stove pipe, about 20 cm (8") above the top plate, helps you judge: normal is approx. 300° C (550°F), and it must not exceed 450° C (750°F).

Detectors

Morsø recommends a smoke detector in the stove room. Some areas require smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. Put at least one smoke detector on each floor, near bedrooms and away from the stove, so reloading doesn't set it off.

care.title: Care & the off-season
care.html:
Wear safety goggles and gloves for any maintenance, and use only original Morsø spare parts.

Paint

The finish is heat-resistant Senotherm paint. Clean it with a vacuum's soft brush attachment or a lint-free cloth. If it turns slightly gray over time, Morsø touch-up spray paint renews it; it smells as it cures on the next fire, so ventilate the room.

Door gasket

The gasket around the door can harden. Replace it if the door gets hard to close, or air leaks in around it and the fire is harder to control. Your stove supplier has a Morsø rope gasket kit.

Before each heating season

Clean the chimney and connector thoroughly and check them for damage. Check the gaskets for wear, the glass for cracks, and the door and handle for tightness.

Over the summer

Clean the stove out thoroughly and leave the air control slightly open. Ash left inside soaks up moisture, which causes rust. Fit a chimney cap to keep rain out, but don't block the flue completely. A desiccant such as kitty litter in the ash pan helps; remove it before the heating season.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Morsø offers a 10-Year Manufacturers Guarantee against manufacturing defects in any of the main exterior body parts. It applies when the stove was supplied by an authorised Morsø dealer.

Not covered

  • The flame-path parts, which take the full heat of the fire and may need replacing as routine maintenance: ashpan, grate, firebricks, cast iron fire plates, glass, baffle and flue collar.
  • The ceramic rope.
  • The paint finish.

Service parts come from your Morsø dealer. Replace damaged parts as soon as possible to avoid further damage.

For the full guarantee terms and to register your new stove online, use the web address on the manual's guarantee page.

specFlue.title: Flue & chimney
specFlue.html:
Min. chimney / connector ID6 inches (or equivalent cross section)
US chimneyUL-103-1985 HT (2100º F.) or code-approved masonry with flue liner
Canada chimneyULC S-629 HT (650ºC)
Heightat least 16 feet recommended (not required), flue collar to top

One flueway per appliance: do not connect to a chimney flue serving any other appliance. Don't oversize; too large a section lets flue gases cool, causing sluggish or unpredictable performance. Secure the flue system independently; it must not rely on the stove for support. Roof construction, large trees nearby and high altitude can affect draft and height. Typical installations are shown only as a diagram on this page.

specConnector.title: Chimney connector
specConnector.html:
Diameter6 inches (150mm)
Single-wall24 MSG black or blue; 24 gauge or heavier steel
Double-walltested and listed for solid-fuel appliances
Horizontal run3 feet (1 metre) max., recommended
Total lengthno longer than 8 feet (2.5 metres)
Slopeup 1/4 inch per foot (20 mm per metre) toward the chimney
Turnsno more than two 90 degree
Horizontal run to ceiling18 inches

No galvanized connector. At least three screws to the stove and to each adjoining section. Use mild bends (45º vs. 90º), form one continuous section, and keep every part accessible for cleaning. Never through an attic, closet or similar concealed space; avoid combustible walls and ceilings (local codes and the chimney manufacturer's instructions apply; in Canada, CAN/CSA-B365). The flue collar is placed in the firebox area.

specRoom.title: Room & air supply
specRoom.html:
Furniture30 inches recommended minimum
Movable combustibles30 inches
Fresh-air inlet2 square inches (1250 square mm) free air space
Mobile homedo not install

A dedicated fresh-air inlet is needed unless enough air leaks in through doorways, windows and the like; it matters most in a well-sealed room or where an extractor hood or ventilation system disturbs the air pressure. Not on a wall usually under negative pressure from normal wind, and not directly across the room from the stove (cold draft). Do not connect the stove to any air distribution duct or system. Protect the stove with an acid-proof cover when acid-washing nearby masonry.
